primitives.name: classifyCommand
primitives.when: Reach for this to tier a shell command's blast radius BEFORE running it — e.g. to pick how much ceremony your human channel demands. Use it standalone when you want the tiering without a Gate; inside a Gate, set `bash: { classify: true }` instead and the gate calls it for you.
primitives.fails: Never throws on its own: a non-string or empty `command` returns `"safe"`, an unknown `platform` falls back to the host's, and non-array `extra*` options are ignored. A `reclassify` callback you supply is called unguarded, so if IT throws the throw propagates. Best-effort and defeatable by construction (base64, heredocs, inline interpreter code) — a speed bump, never a sandbox.
primitives.example:
import { classifyCommand } from "bareguard";
classifyCommand("git status");        // "safe"
classifyCommand("rm -rf build");      // "destructive"
classifyCommand("sudo rm -rf /");     // "super_destructive"

primitives.name: defaultAuditPath
primitives.when: Only to find out WHERE the audit log will land before a Gate exists — e.g. to print the path in a CLI banner, or to tail it. The Gate resolves this itself when you pass no `audit.filePath`.
primitives.fails: Never throws — a pure path computation; it touches no filesystem and creates nothing. Resolves in order: `XDG_STATE_HOME`, then `~/.local/state`, then the current working directory.
primitives.example:
import { defaultAuditPath } from "bareguard";
defaultAuditPath("run-7f3a"); // absolute path to the per-family JSONL log

primitives.name: DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS
primitives.when: Read it to see exactly what bareguard calls tier 2 (loss of a named target) on your platform, or to compose your own set on top. Already built in to `classifyCommand`; you do not pass it.
primitives.signature: DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS: { common: RegExp[], linux: RegExp[], darwin: RegExp[], win32: RegExp[] }
primitives.fails: Plain data; reading never throws. Not frozen — treat it as read-only, since mutating it changes tiering for every Gate in the process.
primitives.example:
import { DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS } from "bareguard";
DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS.win32.length; // what tier 2 means on Windows

primitives.name: Gate
primitives.when: Start here — this IS the chokepoint. Construct one per agent run, `await init()`, then `check()` every action before it runs and `record()` what it cost. Every other export in this package is a piece of this or a helper around it.
primitives.fails: Throws at CONSTRUCTION on malformed config — a section that is not a plain object, or an array-shaped key (`tools.allowlist`, `bash.denyPatterns`, …) that is not an array. A config typo fails CLOSED rather than silently gating nothing. After construction a policy stop is a returned `outcome`, never a throw; `check()` resolves to a terminal allow/deny and never returns `askHuman` (it resolves that internally through `humanChannel`).

primitives.name: globToRegex
primitives.when: Only to mirror bareguard's own glob matching outside the gate — previewing which tools an allowlist admits, or testing a pattern you are about to configure. Supports `*` ONLY (matching any character, including `/` and newlines): no `?`, no character classes, no escapes.
primitives.fails: Throws a `SyntaxError` only if the escaped pattern is not a valid RegExp; ordinary glob input never does. Regex metacharacters in the input are escaped for you, so `"a.b"` matches the literal `a.b`.

primitives.name: INTERPRETER_PATTERNS
primitives.when: Opt in to a coarse speed-bump on inline interpreter code (`python3 -c`, `node -e`, `php -r`) by passing it as `extraDestructive`. Deliberately in NO default set: the same action via `python3 script.py` stays `safe`, so a default escalation would be a false-positive flip for every consumer without closing the hole.
primitives.fails: Frozen, so a mutation attempt throws in strict mode instead of silently changing every Gate in the process. Reading it never throws.
primitives.example:
import { classifyCommand, INTERPRETER_PATTERNS } from "bareguard";
classifyCommand("python3 -c 'import shutil'", { extraDestructive: INTERPRETER_PATTERNS }); // "destructive"

primitives.name: matchAny
primitives.when: The one you usually want over `globToRegex` — test a name against a list of patterns the way `tools.allowlist` / `fs.deny` do. Use it to preview a config, not to enforce; enforcement is the Gate's job.
primitives.fails: Never throws for ordinary input; a missing or empty `globs` returns `false` (no match), which is why an EMPTY `tools.allowlist` is handled by the gate rather than here.

primitives.name: PAYLOAD_FIELDS
primitives.when: Read it to see which `action.args` fields `content` patterns deliberately do NOT scan — the write payload (the document being written), as opposed to the operation. Check it when a deny you expected did not fire on file contents.
primitives.fails: Frozen: an accidental push throws in strict mode rather than silently changing matching for every Gate in the process. There is no config knob — the scoping is fixed at the library.
primitives.example:
import { PAYLOAD_FIELDS } from "bareguard";
PAYLOAD_FIELDS; // ["content", "contents"] — a literal DROP TABLE inside these is not a deny

primitives.name: redact
primitives.when: Only when you are writing your OWN log or human-channel payload and need the same scrubbing the audit line gets. The Gate already redacts every audit line by default — you do not call this to protect the audit.
primitives.fails: Never throws, by contract: it runs inside every audit emit, so a throw would stop the gate dead on every later action. A falsy or non-JSON-serializable value comes back unchanged, and a malformed `secrets` config falls back to the built-in defaults rather than erroring. Non-mutating — the original object is never touched, so policy still evaluates the real action.

primitives.name: routeAnnotation
primitives.when: Only when you are building the Axis-B path by hand and need to know where a fact WOULD go before you pay to compute it. `gate.annotate()` already routes internally, so most callers never call this directly.
primitives.fails: Never throws and has no side effects — it is a pure four-way lookup over three booleans. Any `knob` value other than `"strict"` behaves as `"relaxed"`.

primitives.name: SAFE_DEFAULT_ASK_PATTERNS
primitives.when: Read it to see what `content` escalates to a human at zero config, or spread it into your own `content.askPatterns` to keep the defaults and add to them.
primitives.fails: Plain data; reading never throws. Not frozen — treat it as read-only. These raise an ask, never a deny, and the deny step runs first.
primitives.example:
import { Gate, SAFE_DEFAULT_ASK_PATTERNS } from "bareguard";
new Gate({ content: { askPatterns: [...SAFE_DEFAULT_ASK_PATTERNS, /\bdeploy\b/i] } });

primitives.name: SAFE_DEFAULT_DENY_PATTERNS
primitives.when: Read it to see what `content` denies outright at zero config, or spread it into your own `content.denyPatterns` when you want the defaults PLUS your own. Omitting the config entirely already applies these.
primitives.fails: Plain data; reading never throws. Not frozen — treat it as read-only. These guard destructive OPERATIONS, not payload VALUES, and never scan the fields in `PAYLOAD_FIELDS`.
primitives.example:
import { Gate, SAFE_DEFAULT_DENY_PATTERNS } from "bareguard";
new Gate({ content: { denyPatterns: [...SAFE_DEFAULT_DENY_PATTERNS, /\bALTER\s+TABLE\b/i] } });

primitives.name: SUPER_DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS
primitives.when: Read it to see exactly what bareguard calls tier 3 on your platform, or to compose your own set on top. You do not pass it to `classifyCommand` — it is already the built-in tier-3 set.
primitives.signature: SUPER_DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS: { common: RegExp[], linux: RegExp[], darwin: RegExp[], win32: RegExp[] }
primitives.fails: Plain data; reading never throws. Not frozen — treat it as read-only, since mutating it changes tiering for every Gate in the process.
primitives.example:
import { SUPER_DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS } from "bareguard";
SUPER_DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS.common.some((re) => re.test(cmd)); // is this irrecoverable?
